fields.foundation: The New Kingdom began with the expulsion of the Hyksos, an Asiatic dynasty that had controlled Lower Egypt for over a century during the Second Intermediate Period. Ahmose I, founding pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty, completed this expulsion around 1550 BCE, reunited the country, reconquered Nubian territories lost during the preceding fragmentation, and began rebuilding the administrative and military institutions that would sustain the empire for nearly five centuries. His successors pressed aggressively outward: Thutmose I crossed the Euphrates, the first pharaoh to do so, and carried Egyptian arms beyond the fourth Nile cataract in Nubia. Hatshepsut, who ruled as pharaoh alongside the young Thutmose III from approximately 1479 to 1458 BCE, consolidated this inheritance through trade rather than war. She sent the celebrated expedition to Punt and sponsored a large building programme at Karnak and Deir el-Bahari. Her death in 1458 BCE was followed by a rebellion of Canaanite and Syrian rulers led by the king of Kadesh, who evidently doubted the resolve of her successor. Thutmose III would prove the most consequential military pharaoh in Egyptian history, and the golden age of Amenhotep III rested on the territory that he conquered.
fields.socioeconomy: The New Kingdom economy rested on three things: Nubian gold, Levantine tribute, and agricultural surplus from the Nile floodplain. Nubian gold in particular paid for the empire: it funded monumental construction, sustained diplomatic gift exchanges with Near Eastern powers, and maintained the army. The temple complexes, most prominently Karnak and Luxor, were at once religious centres, economic institutions, and state treasuries. They accumulated land, livestock, and labour obligations on a scale that eventually made the Amun priesthood a rival power to the crown. By the reign of Ramesses III, according to the Great Harris Papyrus, the temples of Amun held roughly two-thirds of all temple lands in Egypt and some ninety percent of temple-owned ships. The state took a direct part in long-distance trade, as in Hatshepsut's Punt expedition, which brought back myrrh trees, ebony, ivory, and exotic animals. Under a policy begun by Thutmose III, the sons of conquered rulers were raised as Egyptians at the pharaonic court. This had both diplomatic and economic ends, producing a class of Egyptianised client princes who governed peripheral territories at minimal cost to the crown.
fields.military: Thutmose III is the leading military figure of the New Kingdom. He conducted some seventeen campaigns over twenty years, beginning with his decisive victory at the Battle of Megiddo in 1457 BCE. There he marched through the narrow Aruna pass to surprise a coalition of Canaanite rulers led by the king of Kadesh, accepting a high risk for the sake of a decisive result. The chariot, introduced into Egyptian warfare during the Hyksos period and afterwards developed for use in combination with other arms, was the main instrument of New Kingdom expansion. The largest single engagement of the era was the Battle of Kadesh in 1274 BCE, where Ramesses II led an estimated 20,000 soldiers against the Hittite king Muwatalli II and his thousands of chariots. The battle was tactically indecisive. The peace treaty of 1258 BCE, concluded with Muwatalli's successor Hattusili III and the earliest such treaty to survive in both parties' versions, in effect acknowledged a strategic stalemate. The empire's final military test came under Ramesses III, who repelled land and sea invasions by the Sea Peoples around 1177 BCE, preserving Egypt while almost every other Bronze Age power collapsed or contracted.
fields.governance: The New Kingdom was administered through a centralised pharaonic system in which the king was at once divine ruler, supreme judge, and commander-in-chief. Two viziers, one for Upper and one for Lower Egypt, managed day-to-day administration, overseeing taxation, judicial proceedings, and the distribution of state resources. Provincial governors administered the nomes, while the Viceroy of Kush, the King's Son of Kush, governed Nubia as a semi-autonomous administration within the empire. The Amarna Letters, the diplomatic archive recovered from Akhenaten's capital, show an organised system of international correspondence conducted in Akkadian cuneiform, through which Egypt managed its relationships with Babylon, Mitanni, Assyria, the Hittites, and Alashiya (Cyprus). Akhenaten's reign, from approximately 1353 to 1336 BCE, was the most disruptive crisis of government in the empire's history. He raised the Aten above all other gods, suppressed the Amun cult, and moved the capital to Akhetaten. The result was religious upheaval at home and diplomatic drift abroad, with Levantine vassals repeatedly requesting Egyptian military assistance against Hittite-backed rivals and receiving little response.
fields.impact: The New Kingdom set the terms of culture, diplomacy, and commerce in the Late Bronze Age Near East. In the Amarna diplomatic system, great powers exchanged elaborate gifts and correspondence to maintain equilibrium; it was the most developed framework for inter-state relations the ancient world had yet produced. Egyptian artistic styles, religious concepts, and architectural forms spread across Canaan, Nubia, and the Levant through conquest, trade, and the deliberate Egyptianisation of foreign elites. Nubia under New Kingdom administration was changed so thoroughly that the later Kushite kingdom centred on Napata adopted Egyptian gods, titles, and monumental forms, and would eventually conquer Egypt itself as the Twenty-Fifth Dynasty. The disintegration of the Bronze Age trading network amid the upheavals of around 1200 BCE permanently undermined the New Kingdom's economic foundations, which shows how far the empire's prosperity depended on the wider Mediterranean commercial system.
fields.decline: The New Kingdom declined gradually, through three processes that came together. The Bronze Age Collapse from approximately 1200 BCE severed the trade networks that sustained imperial revenues and removed the Hittite rival around whom Egyptian foreign policy had been organised. At the same time the Amun priesthood at Thebes steadily accumulated land and institutional power, and became a theocratic counter-authority that the weakened Twentieth Dynasty pharaohs could not suppress. Ramesses III was assassinated by harem conspirators around 1153 BCE, an event documented in the Judicial Papyrus of Turin and supported by forensic examination of his mummy. He was followed by a succession of short-lived rulers who bore his name but had little of his ability. By approximately 1080 BCE, the High Priest of Amun Herihor governed Upper Egypt as a de facto independent ruler, while Smendes controlled Lower Egypt from Tanis. The death of Ramesses XI around 1070 BCE ended the New Kingdom not through conquest but through administrative dissolution.
fields.summary: The Egyptian New Kingdom shows that imperial greatness rested as much on diplomacy and the splendour of a culture as on military conquest.
fields.teaser: The New Kingdom saw Egypt reach the height of its imperial power, with warrior pharaohs like Thutmose III and Ramesses II expanding into Nubia and the Levant.
fields.t0: Egypt's imperial age, founded when Ahmose I expelled the Hyksos c. 1550 BCE, stretched from Nubia to the Euphrates.
fields.t1: Nubian gold, Levantine tribute and the Amarna letters' great-power diplomacy made Egypt the hub of the Late Bronze Age world.
fields.t2: It ended not by conquest but by dissolution, as the Bronze Age Collapse and the rising Amun priesthood hollowed out royal power.
fields.dyk: Ramesses II and the Hittites made peace in 1258 BCE in the earliest treaty to survive in both parties' versions, settling a stalemate after the Battle of Kadesh.
